abstract: Human papillomaviruses (HPVs) are a diverse family of viruses with over 450 members that have been identified and fully sequenced. They are classified into five phylogenetic genera: alpha, beta, gamma, mu, and nu. The high-risk alpha HPVs, such as HPV16, have been studied the most extensively due to their medical significance as cancer-causing agents. However, while nearly 70% of all HPVs are members of the gamma genus, they are almost entirely unstudied. This is because gamma HPVs have been considered medically irrelevant commensals as most of them infect the skin and are not known to cause significant clinical lesions in immunocompetent individuals. Members of the gamma 6 HPVs, however, have been detected in the anogenital tract mucosa and HPV101 has been isolated from a premalignant cervical lesion. Moreover, gamma 6 HPVs have a unique genome structure. They lack E6 proteins but in place of E6, they encode unique, small hydrophobic proteins without any close viral or cellular homologs that have been termed E10. Here, we report that HPV101 E7 shares biochemical activities with the high-risk alpha HPV16 E7, including the ability to target the pRB and PTPN14 tumor suppressors for degradation. This study underscores the importance of further characterizing HPV101 and other unstudied HPV species.

Table S1

GAPDH

Table S1

27

GSE121906

Introduction
Over 450 Human papillomaviruses (HPVs) have been identified and fully sequenced [
1
]. They are classified into five phylogenetic genera: alpha, beta, gamma, mu, and nu. Members of the alpha genus have been studied most extensively because they can be classified as high-risk or low-risk based on the propensity of the lesions that they cause to undergo malignant progression. High-risk HPVs such HPV16 cause lesions that can progress to cancers and cause a large percentage of anogenital tract and oropharyngeal carcinomas [
2
,
3
]. Low-risk HPVs such as HPV6, however, cause anogenital and oral lesions that only rarely undergo malignant progression [
4
,
5
]. While nearly 70% HPVs are members of the gamma genus [
1
], they have not been studied extensively. This is because gamma HPVs have not been considered medically relevant as most of them infect cutaneous epithelia and they are not known to cause significant clinical lesions in immunocompetent individuals [
6
,
7
]. However, this may not be the case for all the members of this large and heterogenous genus.
Among the gamma HPVs, members of the gamma 6 species are notable for several reasons. First, the gamma 6 HPVs have been isolated from the anogenital tract mucosa and hence they may be sexually transmitted [
[8]
,
[9]
,
[10]
,
[11]
]. Second, two of the gamma 6 HPVs, HPV108 and HPV101 have been isolated from low-grade and high-grade cervical intraepithelial lesions, respectively [
8
,
9
]. This suggests the possibility that they may be linked to disease, as these lesions are typically associated with infection by high-risk alpha HPVs. Third, gamma 6 HPVs have a unique genome structure. Nearly all HPVs encode E6 and E7 proteins, which are accessory proteins that enable viral genome synthesis in terminally differentiated epithelial cells [
12
]. Some HPVs express E5 transmembrane proteins that also promote the viral life cycle [
13

[8]
,
[9]
,
[10]
,
[11]
,
14
].
This study seeks to generate insight into the biochemical properties and biological activities of the E7 protein encoded by HPV101, a member of the gamma 6 HPV species that was isolated from a high-grade premalignant cervical lesion [
8
]. We show that HPV101 E7 shares some biological activities and cellular targets with the high-risk alpha HPV16 E7 oncoprotein. These include binding and targeting the pRB and PTPN14 tumor suppressors for degradation, activating E2F-regulated genes, and increasing the expression of the p16
INK4A
tumor suppressor. Our findings underscore the importance of further characterizing HPV101 and other unstudied HPVs.

Fig. 1

HPV101 E7 binds and targets pRB for proteasome-mediated degradation
Given that our AP/MS analysis showed evidence for pRB binding by HPV101 E7, we confirmed and validated this interaction by immunoprecipitation/western blot experiments. We first confirmed the binding of HPV101 E7 and pRB in HCT116 cells by transient co-transfection with FLAG/HA epitope-tagged HPV101 E7 and HA epitope-tagged pRB (
Fig. 2
A). We further validated the HPV101 E7/pRB interaction in immortalized normal human oral keratinocytes (NOKs) with stable expression of FLAG/HA epitope-tagged HPV101 E7 (
Fig. 2
B). Immunoprecipitation of high-risk alpha HPV16 E7 with pRB was included as a positive control. These experiments also showed that the steady state levels of pRB in whole cell extracts of HPV101 E7 expressing NOKs were consistently lower than in control cells, suggesting that like the HPV16 E7 protein, HPV101 E7 may decrease steady-state levels of pRB (
Fig. 2
A and B). To corroborate this finding, we performed additional western blot experiments in primary human foreskin keratinocytes (HFKs) with stable expression of FLAG/HA epitope-tagged HPV101 E7. HFKs with stable expression of FLAG/HA epitope-tagged HPV16 E7 were used as positive controls. Consistent with the results with HPV101 E7-expressing NOKs, pRB levels were also reduced in HPV101 E7-expressing HFKs to a similar extent as in HPV16 E7-expressing HFKs (
Fig. 2
C). The pRB/HPV101 E7 complex proved difficult to detect by immunoprecipitation/western blot experiments, presumably due to the lower pRB levels in the extracts from HPV101 E7 expressing cells. HPV16 E7 decreases pRB steady state levels by targeting it for proteasome-mediated degradation [
38
,
39
]. To determine if HPV101 E7 functions similarly, we transiently transfected Saos-2 human osteosarcoma cells, which lack detectable pRB, with exogenous pRB and HPV101 E7 or HPV16 E7 as a positive control [
39
]. Following transfection, we treated these cells with Bortezomib, a proteasome inhibitor, for 16 h. In the absence of Bortezomib, pRB protein levels were dramatically reduced in Saos-2 cells expressing HPV101 E7 or HPV16 E7 (
Fig. 2
D), further corroborating our findings in NOKs and primary HFKs (
Fig. 2
B and C). Bortezomib treatment increased pRB steady state levels in cells that expressed HPV101 E7 or HPV16 E7, which supports the model that like HPV16 E7, HPV101 E7 targets pRB for degradation by the proteasome (
Fig. 2
D). Hence, we conclude that HPV101 E7 shares the ability of HPV16 E7 to interact with and reduce pRB steady state levels by targeting it for proteasome-mediated degradation.

Discussion
Unlike other members of the gamma genus which infect cutaneous epithelia, the known members of the gamma 6 HPVs have been isolated from the anogenital tract mucosa [
[8]
,
[9]
,
[10]
,
[11]
]. Moreover, they have a unique genomic structure with the E6 ORF replaced by E10 that encodes a small, hydrophobic protein [
[8]
,
[9]
,
[10]
,
[11]
,
14
]. In this study, we focused on HPV101, which has been detected in a high-grade premalignant cervical lesion [
8
]. To determine whether HPV101 may have oncogenic activities, we investigated the biochemical and biological activities of the HPV101 E7 protein, which in the case of the cancer-associated, high-risk alpha HPVs, is a major oncogenic driver [
12
]. We found that HPV101 E7 shares several activities with high-risk HPV16 E7 that are critical for its ability to enable oncogenic transformation of infected cells. These include binding and targeting pRB and PTPN14 for proteasomal degradation, activating E2F-regulated gene transcription, and inducing expression of p16
INK4A
. Moreover, HPV101 E7 and HPV16 E7 proteins cause similar alterations to the host cell transcriptome. In contrast to HPV16 E7, however, HPV101 E7 expression does not markedly enhance the proliferative capacity of primary HFKs under the conditions used in these experiments. There are several possible explanations for this. One, HPV101 E7 may less efficiently cause pRB and/or PTPN14 degradation than HPV16 E7. Notably, low-risk mucosal HPV E7 proteins have been reported to less efficiently degrade PTPN14 than high-risk HPV E7 proteins [
42
,
43
,
54
]. There might also be additional HPV16 E7 activities that contribute to the enhanced proliferative capacity of primary HFKs that are not shared with HPV101 E7. For example, HPV101 E7 lacks the AP2 binding site as well as a CK2 phosphorylation site. The ability of HPV16 E7 to bind AP2 has been linked to transformation, particularly under conditions of limiting nutrients [
35
,
55
] and similarly, CK2 phosphorylation has also been linked to the oncogenic activities of high-risk mucosal HPVs [
56
,
57
].
Gamma HPVs comprise nearly 70% of all HPVs that have been fully sequenced [
1
]. Because gamma HPVs have historically been considered commensal cutaneous papillomaviruses with little medical relevance, they have not been extensively studied [
6
,
7
]. However, there is a growing list of gamma HPVs that have been linked to pathologies of various anatomical sites. One such virus is HPV197, a member of the gamma 24 species, which was reported as the most frequently detected HPV in skin cancers [
58
]. A previous study from our group determined that, despite lacking the canonical LXCXE pRB binding motif, the HPV197 E7 protein shares important cellular interactors with high-risk alpha as well as beta HPV E7 proteins including UBR4/p600 and pRB [
22
]. While HPV197 E7 was shown to bind pRB and activate E2F-regulated gene transcription, there was no evidence that it decreased pRB steady-state levels. Another finding from the proteomic analysis in this study was that there was no evidence for HPV197 E7 to be able to associate with the pRB-related, p107/RBL1 and p130/RBL2 proteins, and only a single unique peptide was detected for PTPN14 [
22
]. In contrast, we show here that HPV101 E7 can bind pRB, p107/RBL1, p130/RBL2, UBR4, and PTPN14, and similar to high-risk HPV16 E7, it can target pRB and PTPN14 for degradation. This is just one example of the differences among the various species of the gamma HPVs. Hence, it is important to study more of them to better understand their unique biochemical and biological activities.
In addition to elucidating similarities and differences between the E7 interactomes of various HPV species, our study and others have identified novel common interactors. For example, we noted two cellular proteins that commonly interact with the beta 1 HPV8, gamma 24 HPV197, and gamma 6 HPV101 proteins. The first is Polymerase I and transcript release factor (PTRF) or Cavin-1 [
[59]
,
[60]
,
[61]
], which has been shown to contribute to sustained proliferation, migration, and anchorage-independent growth of rhabdomyosarcoma cells [
62
]. The other is WW Domain-Containing Protein 2 (WWC2), a member of the WW-and-C2-domain-containing protein family which consists of WWC1 (KIBRA), WWC2 and WWC3 [
63
]. WWC proteins are upstream components of the Hippo signaling pathway which regulates cell differentiation and proliferation as well as organ growth control [
64
,
65
]. Aberrations in WWC expression and activity has been linked to cancer development [
65
]. HPVs are known to subvert Hippo signaling by targeting PTPN14 for degradation which results in YAP1 activation [
44
]. Therefore, it will be interesting to further investigate the potential physical and functional interactions of WWC2 with HPV E7 proteins. These findings further underscore the value of performing unbiased proteomic analyses of E6 and E7 proteins from many different HPV species to uncover interactions that may have biological relevance [
66
].

,
[9]

[10]
,
[11]

8
,
14

14
]. Since all known gamma 6 HPVs were isolated from anogenital mucosal samples, they likely adapted to the mucosal niche [
14

9

CIP1
[
9

9
]. However, many of these conclusions were drawn from morphological observation of spontaneously immortalized human foreskin keratinocytes (NIKS) [
67

Nonetheless, given that all gamma 6 HPVs have been isolated from the anogenital tract mucosa, it is important to determine whether they have oncogenic activities because such viruses may repopulate these and other mucosal epithelial niches once the alpha genus and low- and high-risk HPVs are eliminated by vaccinations. The exact prevalence of gamma 6 HPVs in the anogenital tract mucosa is difficult to assess because they are detected by RNA-seq, not traditional PCR-based methods. Thus, it is critical to study HPV types that are currently considered “rare”, such as the gamma 6 HPVs to accurately assess the risk they pose as etiological agents.
Future experiments will focus on determining whether the biological consequences of HPV101 E7-and HPV16 E7-mediated pRB and PTPN14 degradation are similar, whether HPV101 E7 expression triggers the activation of the p53 tumor suppressor, and which signaling pathways may be required for HPV101 E7 to efficiently enhance the proliferative capacity of primary human keratinocytes. The biochemical and biological activities of the E10 protein are unknown and it will be important to elucidate its role in the viral lifecycle and to determine if it compensates for the lack of E6 in gamma 6 HPVs. Our study did not investigate whether the capability of HPV101 E7 to bind and degrade PTPN14 affects keratinocyte differentiation. Nonetheless, our findings contribute to the growing body of evidence suggesting that certain gamma HPVs, traditionally considered non-pathogenic, may play more active roles in disease than previously assumed.
